newsitem.title: CANADA: Gulf says move to gain access to capital.
newsitem.headline: Gulf says move to gain access to capital.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, which said earlier today it was moving its senior executives to Denver from Calgary, is making the change to gain better access to bigger capital markets and more international oil deals, a Gulf spokesman said on Wednesday.

"We've made it pretty clear that we're going to expand internationally and the feeling among our leadership group is that being in Denver will help us do that without being all that far away from Calgary," Gulf's John Sparks said in a phone interview from New York.

Gulf said it planned to move 20 of its 25 corporate staff, including chief executive J.P. Bryan, to Denver by April 1, 1997. The company plans to maintain its Calgary office as home base for North American operations.

Sparks said executives of Gulf Canada, whose predecessor company British American Oil was founded in Canada in 1906, spent much of their time meeting with institutional investors in major U.S. centers such as New York, San Francisco and New Orleans. Denver was a logical hub, he said.

Bryan, a flamboyant Texan who gained control of struggling Gulf in 1995 with a C$300 million cash infusion, has said that Canadian investment analysts had not given the company its due for opportunities created from a major restructuring.
He has said that Gulf's troubled history, especially as part of the ill-fated Olympia and York empire, made Canadian analysts wary of of its stock, leading to lower valuations than deserved.
Bryan has also conceded that since arriving on the Canadian oil scene, he had not been fully accepted by the tight-knit Calgary energy community.

Gulf's corporate move runs counter to a trend that over the past year has seen several large corporations, such as Canadian Pacific Ltd unit CP Rail and Suncor Inc, pull up stakes in eastern Canada and relocate in the Alberta city.
Meanwhile, Denver and the Rocky Mountain west, hard hit when oil prices fell in the late 1980s, lost numerous well-paying jobs in the oil industry.
